title: A 30-Year Harvard Study Found the Exact Amount of Strength Training That Lowers Death Risk. It Is Less Than You Think.
excerpt: Ninety to 120 minutes per week cut cardiovascular mortality by 19 per cent and neurological death by 27 per cent. Beyond that, the returns flatlined.
body:
A 30-year Harvard study tracking 147,374 Americans has identified a precise weekly window of strength training that delivers the greatest protection against early death. The research, published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, found that 90 to 120 minutes of resistance exercise per week was associated with a 13 per cent lower risk of dying from any cause.

The study drew on three major longitudinal health surveys — the Health Professionals Follow-up Study, the Nurses' Health Study, and the Nurses' Health Study II — spanning data collected between 1992 and 2022. Participants reported their exercise habits every two years, covering activities like squats, lunges, push-ups, and weight lifting alongside aerobic pursuits such as running, swimming, and cycling.

The Sweet Spot Is Surprisingly Modest

During the study period, 35,798 participants died. After adjusting for age, lifestyle, and pre-existing health conditions, the data pointed to a clear threshold: people who maintained 90 to 119 minutes of strength training per week saw a 19 per cent reduction in cardiovascular death and a striking 27 per cent drop in mortality from neurological diseases, including Alzheimer's and dementia.

Crucially, pushing beyond 120 minutes per week did not yield additional protection. "The benefits appear to level off rather than continue increasing," the researchers noted, suggesting that consistency matters more than volume.

The relationship with cancer was less straightforward. The strongest reduction in cancer mortality — 21 per cent — appeared at much lower levels, between 1 and 29 minutes per week. Researchers cautioned against reading this as evidence that less exercise is better, saying the pattern needs further investigation.

Combining Strength and Cardio Delivers the Biggest Returns

The study's most powerful finding emerged when researchers examined people who did both resistance training and aerobic exercise. Those who met the recommended 150 minutes per week of moderate aerobic activity while also lifting weights saw their risk of premature death drop by up to 58 per cent — far exceeding the benefit of either form of exercise alone.

This aligns with emerging consensus that the two exercise types work on the body in fundamentally different ways. Aerobic activity strengthens the heart and lungs, while resistance training builds muscle mass, preserves bone density, and maintains physical function — a combination that becomes increasingly critical after middle age.

Why This Matters for South Asian Families

The findings carry particular weight for the South Asian diaspora. Type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and sarcopenia — the age-related loss of muscle mass — all disproportionately affect people of South Asian descent. Studies have consistently shown that South Asians develop metabolic risk at lower body weights and earlier ages than European populations.

Yet cultural norms in many Indian households have traditionally favoured walking, yoga, and flexibility-based exercise over weight training. The perception that lifting heavy is only for bodybuilders or young athletes persists, particularly among older adults and women.

This study challenges that thinking directly. Three sessions of 30 to 40 minutes per week — using dumbbells, resistance bands, or even bodyweight exercises at home — falls squarely within the protective window.

What Comes Next

The researchers acknowledged limitations: the data is observational, meaning it shows association rather than definitive cause. Participants were predominantly health professionals, which may limit how broadly the findings apply. But the sheer scale — nearly 150,000 people over three decades — makes it one of the most comprehensive examinations of strength training and longevity ever conducted.

For NRI families watching their parents age across continents and managing their own metabolic risk in sedentary desk jobs, the message is uncomfortably clear. Walking is good. Yoga is good. But if you are not picking up something heavy at least twice a week, you are leaving years on the table.
